tagline: A slender strip from sea to savanna
overview:
Togo is a ribbon of a country in West Africa, only about 110 kilometers wide at its broadest but stretching some 550 kilometers inland from a short Atlantic coast. Squeezed between Ghana and Benin, with Burkina Faso to the north, it is roughly the size of West Virginia. The capital, Lomé, sits right on the beach in the southwestern corner, so close to Ghana that the border runs along the edge of the city, and its port serves landlocked countries far inland.

About 9 million people live in Togo, in some 40 ethnic groups; the Ewe are the largest in the south and the Kabye in the north. French is the official language, while Ewe and Kabye are widely spoken at home and in markets. Togo is a republic. Most families farm, growing maize, yams, cassava and cocoa, and phosphate rock for fertilizer is the main mineral export. Togo is also one of the homelands of the Vodun religion.
landAndNature: Sandy beaches and coconut palms line the coast, backed by lagoons and shallow Lake Togo. Inland the ground rises into the Togo Mountains, a green chain of forested hills where Mount Agou reaches 986 meters, the country's highest point, and waterfalls drop through the trees near Kpalimé. Farther north the land flattens into savanna of tall grass and baobab trees, hotter and drier, where the harmattan wind carries Saharan dust each winter. Fazao-Malfakassa and Kéran parks protect elephants, antelope, monkeys and hippos. Butterflies are so numerous in the hills around Kpalimé that collectors and naturalists travel there just to see them.
peopleAndCulture: Togolese meals center on pounded yam or a maize dough called akoumé, eaten with sauces of okra, tomato or peanut, and plenty of fish along the coast. Street stalls sell fried plantain and spicy beans. Music ranges from ceremonial drumming and dance to Afrobeat and reggae in Lomé's bars. Vodun, a religion of spirits and ancestors that began in this region, is practiced alongside Christianity and Islam. In the northeast, the Tamberma build fortified mud houses with rounded towers, protected as a World Heritage site. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Togo reached the World Cup finals in 2006.
history: Ewe, Kabye and other peoples settled this land over many centuries, some moving here to escape wars elsewhere. For roughly 200 years the shore was part of what Europeans called the Slave Coast, a place where captured people were shipped across the Atlantic; the old town of Aného still carries that history. Germany claimed the territory as Togoland in 1884 and built railways and plantations. After World War I it was divided between Britain and France, and the British part later joined Ghana. French Togoland became independent on April 27, 1960. Gnassingbé Eyadéma ruled from 1967 until his death in 2005, one of Africa's longest-serving leaders, and his son took over after him.
funFacts: Togo is one of Africa's narrowest countries, in places only about 50 kilometers from its western to its eastern border.
Lomé is one of the very few capital cities built directly against an international border, in this case with Ghana.
Lomé's Grand Marché was long run by powerful women traders nicknamed the Nana Benz for the cars they drove.
The Tamberma build two-story mud houses with towers and flat roofs that look like small castles in the savanna.
Phosphate rock mined near Togo's coast is shipped worldwide to make fertilizer, and is the country's leading export mineral.
